title: Second molars: Case 1

findings.title: Clinical finding
findings.text: #37 is partially erupted. #47 is more erupted than #37, with more crown showing in the mouth.

phases.title: Observe the records
phases.goal: Describe what you see in the history, clinical findings and records, then say what you think the main problems are and how sure you can be from these records alone.
phases.starterQuestion: Looking through the records, what is the patient's chief complaint, and what do you notice about her malocclusion?
exampleQuestions: What does she mean by a tooth "growing inside"?
At 13, which teeth would you expect to be fully erupted well into the arch that aren't?
Which second molar shows more crown in the mouth, and why does that matter?
Is there anything about the impaction area that would make you treat it sooner?
How would you describe her bite? Note some occlusal findings.

rubric.text: Records the chief complaint, age and growth status.
rubric.revealText: She's 13 and 1.5 years past menarche. Her complaint is about her front teeth, so the impacted molars will most likely be treated as part of comprehensive orthodontic treatment.

rubric.text: Links the "lower tooth growing inside" to the retained #83 with #43 erupted lingually.
rubric.revealText: The lower right primary canine #83, is still there, so #43 has erupted lingually. That's the tooth she's noticed.

rubric.text: Identifies #37 and #47 as mesially impacted rather than simply late, relating her age to the normal eruption time of second molars.
rubric.revealText: At 13, second molars are usually erupted. Both lower second molars are mesially angulated and their mesial marginal ridges are locked under the distal bulge of the first molars at CEJ level. So this is impaction, not just late eruption.

rubric.text: Checks the impaction sites for food trapping, caries and how well she can keep them clean, and uses this to judge urgency.
rubric.revealText: A partially erupted, impacted molar traps food. However, there is no caries seen on the first molar and seems to be able to keep the are clean, so nothing is forcing urgent treatment.

rubric.text: Names at least two relevant occlusal findings: Class II div 1 incisors, increased OJ/OB, crossbite #12/#83, scissors bite #14 and #27, crowding, non-coincident midlines, or the canine and molar relationships.
rubric.revealText: Her incisors are Class II div 1 with increased OJ at 5mm and increased OB at 50%. There is crossbite at #12/#83, scissors bites at #14 and #27, upper mild crowding, moderate lower crowding, and both upper and lower dental midlines deviated to the right.

rubric.text: Notes how much of each second molar crown is exposed, and that this decides whether an attachment can be bonded.
rubric.revealText: #47 shows more crown in the mouth than #37. That matters because you need enough tooth surface to bond a tube before you can upright it, which also points to ease, speed and prognosis of uprighting it.

acceptedExtras.text: Reviews the whole OPG before the teeth: condyles, bone, sinuses, any pathology.
Compares the two sides and notes that #47 looks more favourable than #37.
Considers the opposing occlusion and interocclusal clearance, noting the upper second molars are erupting buccally and #27 is in scissors bite.
Notes all four third molars are present, without making them a requirement in this phase.

tutorGuidance: Keep the recorded context separate from interpretation: she is 13, 1.5 years post-menarche, with no relevant medical history, and caries and periodontally controlled.
Before discussing prognosis or treatment, the student should record the retained #83 with lingual #43, both impacted second molars, and at least two occlusal findings.

The case does not record her stated wish for comprehensive treatment, or the interocclusal clearance. If the student asks, accept it as a sensible question; say her complaint about her front teeth suggests she is open to full treatment, and do not invent a measurement.
The OPG alone can determine the reading of angulation and locking without anterior maxillary occlusal or bitewings radiographs.
No 3D imaging is available for this case. Never suggest or ask about it. If a student asks for it, say it isn't available and ask what the 2D records show.

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students): Experts 1 and 2 (orthodontists): patient's wish for comprehensive treatment, age relative to eruption timing, food trap / caries / hygiene setting urgency, crown exposure for bonding, #47 more crown visible. Expert 1: opposing occlusion and interocclusal clearance. Expert 3 (oral surgeon): holistic OPG review (bonus only).
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.

phases.title: Characterize the impaction
phases.goal: Use the records to describe exactly how each second molar is impacted, and what each record can and can't show you.
phases.starterQuestion: How would you describe the impaction of #37 and #47, and what does each record tell you about it and its surrounding?
exampleQuestions: What do the xrays show about where the crowns of second molar is obstructed against?
Is this impaction mesioangular, horizontal or vertical? Why does that matter?
Which molar sits deeper, and how does that affect treatment?
What do the roots of #37 and #47 tell you about its development?
What about the roots shape and position and how it links to any risks?
Is there space available behind each second molar?
If you moved the second molars back, what might they run into?

rubric.text: Describes the angulation of each molar, classifies it as mesioangular (not horizontal or vertical), and identifies #37 as the more tipped.
rubric.revealText: Both #37 and #47 are impacted with mesial inclination, although #37 has more severe angulation thus impaction. Mesioangular is a more favourable pattern than horizontal.

rubric.text: Describes the vertical depth: the mesial marginal ridge locked under the distal bulge of the first molar at CEJ level.
rubric.revealText: On both sides the mesial marginal ridges are locked under the distal bulge of the first molars at CEJ level. #47 sits slightly higher than #37, which is another reason it may be easier to manage.

rubric.text: Records root development (about two-thirds to almost complete, apices open) and considers root shape and root position.
rubric.revealText: Both roots are two-thirds to almost formed with open ends. There is higher risk to mobility and root resorption for root shape that is short or conical, and root position that is located far distally.

rubric.text: Records third molar position and whether the third molars would get in the way if the second molars were moved back.
rubric.revealText: The lower third molars are present with crowns formed and their roots just starting. It is located behind the second molar roots. If you push the second molar crowns back, they could collide with the third molar teeth.

rubric.text: Considers the space behind each second molar, including how close it is to the ascending ramus.
rubric.revealText: Look at the space available behind each second molar crown and how near it is to the ramus. There’s some room to move the crowns distally in this case as the third molar teeth are developing in that area.

acceptedExtras.text: Distinguishes impaction (a physical obstruction, here the first molar's distal bulge) from primary failure of eruption (no obstruction), and links the cause to prognosis.
Notes the molars are caught mainly against the adjacent tooth rather than buried in bone, which is more favourable.
Checks for a visible periodontal ligament space around the second molars.
Notes the OPG can distort angulation, so the bitewing gives a more reliable view of the contact.

tutorGuidance: Treat the bitewing and OPG findings in the case summary as the source-backed description. Never claim the model read image pixels.
Keep angulation, vertical depth, root development and shape, third molar position and posterior space as separate descriptors.
Root resorption risk cannot be predicted definitively from these records. If asked, the expected answer is to assume it may happen and consent the patient for it.
The case summary does not report caries or resorption on the distal surfaces of #36 and #46. Do not invent findings there. If the student raises it, accept it as a sensible thing to check.
No 3D imaging is available for this case. Do not suggest it. If asked, say it isn't available and redirect to the 2D records.

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students): Experts 1 and 2: angulation (mesioangular more favourable than horizontal or vertical), vertical depth, caries, third molar collision on distalisation, posterior space and ramus, distal root position needing more time, conical roots and resorption risk "assume and consent". Expert 1: #47 more superiorly positioned; aetiology (impaction vs PFE). Expert 2: visible PDL. Expert 3: tooth impaction rather than bony impaction (bonus only).
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.

phases.title: Assess the prognosis
phases.goal: Weigh what makes it more or less likely that each second molar can be uprighted into the arch, and what could go wrong.
phases.starterQuestion: How likely is it that #37 and #47 can be uprighted into the arch, and what makes each more or less likely?
exampleQuestions: What about each molar that makes it easier or harder to upright?
Why might #47 be easier than #37?
How would your view change if she were 30 years old?
Where could the space for uprighting come from?
Would you rather keep the second molars or the wisdom teeth? Why?
What would you warn her about before starting?

rubric.text: Assesses prognosis for each molar from several factors together: angulation, depth, crown exposure for bonding, root development, space and third molar position.
rubric.revealText: Both molars have a good prognosis: they're mesioangular, can be seen in the arch, bondable, caries-free, and the roots are still open. #47 is slightly better because it is more erupted and shows more crown.

rubric.text: Recognises that her age and open apices favour treatment now: the tooth moves more readily and bone and gum heal better in a young patient.
rubric.revealText: At a young age with open root ends, the molars move more easily, and the bone and gum recover better after uprighting.

rubric.text: Links prognosis to space: creating space in front (extractions with first molar mesialisation) makes uprighting easier than relying on distalisation alone.
rubric.revealText: Uprighting is much easier if the first molars can move forward into extraction space. If you can only push the second molars back, the third molars and ramus may limit us.

rubric.text: Recognises that keeping the second molars is preferable to replacing them with the third molars, because third molar size and shape  are still unpredictable at age 13.
rubric.revealText: Second molars are valuable functional units. At 13 the wisdom teeth have barely started forming their roots, so we can't yet tell if they'd make a good replacement. That favours saving the second molars especially if their prognosis is not poor.

rubric.text: Names the main risks of uprighting: root resorption, mobility, a periodontal pocket or bony defect distal to the second molar, and an open contact with food trapping.
rubric.revealText: Risks include root shortening, mobility, deep pocket or bone defect behind the molar, and a gap that traps food. These are less likely in a young patient but should be discussed with her.

acceptedExtras.text: Notes that waiting is unlikely to help: molars locked at CEJ level are unlikely to right themselves.
Notes that her growth stage affects the skeletal side of the plan but does not drive second molar eruption.
Plans a progress checkpoint, with escalation if a molar does not respond.

tutorGuidance: The expert view is that both molars have a good prognosis, with #47 slightly better. Do not describe #37 as poor or guarded.
Assess prognosis from several factors together. Do not reduce it to one factor.
Do not require a specific uprighting technique in this phase. That belongs to Phase 5.
Root resorption risk cannot be measured from the records; accept "assume it may happen and consent the patient".

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students), part 1 of 2: All three experts: prognosis good for both molars, #47 slightly better. Experts 1 and 2: space via lower extractions and first molar mesialisation improves prognosis; keep two molars where possible; risks of resorption, mobility, distal pocket, open contact. Expert 2: perio defects less likely in young patients.

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students), part 2 of 2: Expert 3 (weighted, removal decision): third molar morphology unpredictable at 13, so keep the second molars; younger bone and healing more favourable.
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.

phases.title: Build the problem list
phases.goal: Organise all the patient's problems into a prioritized list, not just the impacted molars.
phases.starterQuestion: Can you put together a prioritised problem list for this patient, ordered from most to least important?
exampleQuestions: If the skeletal base is Class I, where is the Class II overjet coming from?
Where do the impacted molars sit on your list, and why?
Which problems matter most to her?

rubric.text: Identifies the dental Class II div 1 presentation: increased OJ, increased OB, proclined upper incisors, reduced interincisal angle.
rubric.revealText: The upper incisors are proclined, with increased overjet at 5 mm and increased overbite at 50%.

rubric.text: Includes the impacted #37 and #47 and places them high, even though they are not her complaint.
rubric.revealText: The impacted second molars aren't what she's worried about, but they need to be planned for from the start, because they decide how you use space in the lower arch.

rubric.text: Includes the retained #83 with lingual #43, crossbite #12/#83, scissors bites #14 and #27, crowding (upper mild, lower moderate) and non-coincident midlines.
rubric.revealText: Also on the list: retained #84, #43 lingually displaced, crossbite, scissors bite, mild upper crowding, moderate lower crowding, and non-coincident midlines.

acceptedExtras.text: Adds the developing third molars as context, without making them a required item.

tutorGuidance: Keep the Class I skeletal base separate from the dental Class II div 1 incisor presentation. Do not describe her as skeletal Class II.

Include the impacted molars, retained #83 with lingual #43, increased overjet, increased overbite, crowding, midlines and the patient's concerns in one integrated list. It is ok to not be specific with the tooth numbering of crossbite or scissorbite.
Accept the student's order as their prioritisation and do not ask them to rank again. Probe the reasoning, especially if the impacted molars are placed low.
Third molar status is bonus context only.

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students): Expert 2: impacted molars assessed alongside the whole malocclusion, overjet concern, lower crowding, retained #83, midlines and crossbite. Expert 1: breadth of the case (patient factors and the malocclusion the impaction sits in) as the test of understanding.
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.

phases.title: Compare management options
phases.goal: Put forward a treatment plan for both arches that includes the impacted second molars, justify it, and weigh it against the alternatives.
phases.starterQuestion: What treatment plan would you propose for this patient, including the impacted second molars, and why?
exampleQuestions: Which teeth would you extract, and why?
How does your extraction choice in the lower quadrant help the second molars?
Would you keep or remove the lower wisdom teeth? What would decide it?
Why not just extract #37 and let #38 take its place?
How would you upright #37 and #47?

rubric.text: Gives one justified plan addressing both arches: overjet, crowding, lingual #43, crossbite, scissors bites and midlines. An extraction plan is expected given the moderate lower crowding and her overjet concern.
rubric.revealText: With moderate lower crowding and a 5 mm overjet she's worried about, extractions are likely. Taking out #14 and #24 reduces the overjet and removes the #14 scissors bite. In the lower arch, #44 or #45 on the right and #34 or #35 on the left are all reasonable.

rubric.text: Links the lower extraction choice to the second molars: closing extraction space by moving the first molars forward frees room to upright the second molars.
rubric.revealText: Extraction of #35 #45 allow mesialization of #36 #46 which will give more space to align the impacted second molars. Some may choose to extract

rubric.text: Plans to keep and upright both second molars and explains why extracting a second molar is not the preferred option here.
rubric.revealText: Both second molars have a good prognosis and are worth keeping. Extracting one and hoping the wisdom tooth replaces it is less predictable, because at age 13 you can't yet tell how the wisdom tooth will turn out.

rubric.text: Makes and justifies a decision about the lower third molars: keep them if extraction space allows uprighting without much distalisation; remove them if the second molars must move back and the third molars are in the way.
rubric.revealText: If the extraction space lets you upright mostly by moving the roots forward, the wisdom teeth may not need to come out. If you need to push the crowns back, the wisdom teeth will block you and may need removing first.

rubric.text: Describes appropriate uprighting mechanics for a partly erupted molar and how the attachment choice affects them.
rubric.revealText: Bond a tube if there's enough crown, which is easier on #47. Then upright with a stiff base archwire plus a piggyback wire and open coil, or an uprighting spring. Aim to move the roots forward more than the crowns back.

acceptedExtras.text: The part on TAD is bonus.
Notes a TPA is optional, since the overjet is only 5 mm. But it is useful to add on distal extension hook from the TPA to correct scissors bite on #27.
Discusses anchorage: the reaction on the first molars and premolars during uprighting.
Notes that uprighting extrudes the molars, which suits her increased overbite, and checks the interocclusal clearance.
Offers a second plan, for example a non-extraction approach with third molar removal and distalisation, and explains why it is not their Plan A.

tutorGuidance: Require one justified plan covering both arches. A second plan is a bonus.

The orthodontic experts favoured an extraction plan: upper first premolars plus lower premolar extractions, with #44 on the right and #35 (or #34) on the left, using first molar mesialisation to help uprighting. Accept other premolar choices when the student justifies them.

A non-extraction plan with third molar removal and distalisation was suggested by the oral surgeon. Accept it only if the student explains how the moderate lower crowding and the overjet will be corrected; probe this, since the orthodontists did not favour it.

Do not accept extraction of either second molar as the preferred option without challenge. Ask the student to weigh third molar unpredictability at age 13 against keeping a sound second molar and the long term monitoring required.
Accept either keeping or removing the lower third molars when the reasoning ties to the mechanics (root mesialisation vs crown distalisation) and the space available.
Carry forward the Phase 2 findings without adding new ones. No 3D imaging is available for this case.

Full reveal for 5.1 as written by the clinical lead; students see a shortened version (tutor only, never show to students), part 1 of 2: With moderate lower crowding and a 5 mm overjet she's worried about, extractions may be needed to create space. Extraction of upper first premolars (#14 and #24) help with reduction of overjet while also immediately removing the problem of #14 scissors bite.

Full reveal for 5.1 as written by the clinical lead; students see a shortened version (tutor only, never show to students), part 2 of 2: Some may extract #44 to relieve lower right quadrant crowding and align #43, or #45 to help align the impacted #47. Lower left quadrant can be #35 or #34.

Full reveal for 5.5 as written by the clinical lead; students see a shortened version (tutor only, never show to students), part 1 of 2: Bond a tube if there's enough crown, which is easier on #47. Then upright using, for example, a stiff base archwire with a piggyback wire and open coil, or an uprighting spring. Aim for more root movement forward and less crown movement back.

Full reveal for 5.5 as written by the clinical lead; students see a shortened version (tutor only, never show to students), part 2 of 2: TADs can be an option as well, but placing it in the retromolar area may be difficult here with the developing third molars in the way, and if near unattached mucosa it has a risk of being buried in.

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students), part 1 of 2: Experts 1 and 2: extraction plan and first molar mesialisation to create uprighting space; keep both second molars. Expert 2: specific pattern U4s / #44 / #35, #14 extraction relieves the scissors bite, TPA optional, tube preferred, piggyback with open coil or lever arm, retromolar TADs difficult.

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students), part 2 of 2: Expert 1: reduce distalisation and favour root mesialisation where third molars are close; remove third molars if distalisation is needed and there is no room. Expert 3 (weighted, removal decisions): keep the second molars and remove the third molars rather than the second molars, as third molar morphology is unpredictable at 13; his non-extraction view on the overall plan carries less weight.
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.

phases.title: Review the plan
phases.goal: Picture where treatment should end up, work back from that end point, and name the challenges you expect and what would make you change course.
phases.starterQuestion: Picture the end of treatment under your plan. What challenges do you anticipate getting there?
exampleQuestions: Where will each lower molar end up at the end of treatment?
Working back from that end point, is there anything you'd change?
What would you do if the molar isn't responding?
How would you explain the risks of uprighting to her?

rubric.text: Describes the end point and works backwards from it: where each molar, premolar and canine ends up, and the movements needed to get there.
rubric.revealText: At the end, both second molars should be upright in occlusion behind first molars that have moved forward, the overjet reduced, and #43 aligned.

rubric.text: States a reassessment checkpoint for each second molar and what triggers the fallback.
rubric.revealText: To check whether each second molar is actually uprighting after a few months. If not, may need to change mechanics of uprighting or explore other treatment plans.

rubric.text: Acknowledges the main risks: root resorption and mobility, a distal pocket or bony defect needing periodontal care, an open contact with food trapping, and collision with the third molars.
rubric.revealText: The main risks are root shortening and mobility, a deep pocket or bone defect behind the second molar that may need a periodontist, a gap that traps food, and running into the wisdom teeth.

rubric.text: Considers vertical and occlusal effects of uprighting the impacted second molars: extrusion of second molars, reciprocal intrusion/extrusion or tipping of anchorage teeth, and unwanted movement if the cantilever is activated outside the intended plane.
rubric.revealText: Uprighting can extrude the second molars and cause early contacts, tip or move the anchor teeth and change the occlusal plane, or move teeth the wrong way if the spring is activated in the wrong plane.

acceptedExtras.text: Plans long-term monitoring of the remaining third molars after treatment.
Considers retention for the corrected scissors bites and crossbite.
Mentions treatment duration and cost as factors in her choice.

tutorGuidance: Defend an anticipated outcome rather than promising a guaranteed result. Link it to the chosen plan, the evidence and the patient's concerns.
Visualising the end point and working backwards to the mechanics is the skill the experts found hardest to teach. Prompt the student to describe final tooth positions before mechanics.
Make the uprighting checkpoint and fallback explicit for each second molar.
Carry forward the Phase 2 findings without adding new ones. No 3D imaging is available for this case.

Full reveal for 6.4 as written by the clinical lead; students see a shortened version (tutor only, never show to students), part 1 of 2: Uprighting the impacted second molars may have side effects - Extrusion of second molars: uprighting mechanics may introduce an extrusive force component  leading to occlusal interference, premature contact, increased posterior vertical dimension

Full reveal for 6.4 as written by the clinical lead; students see a shortened version (tutor only, never show to students), part 2 of 2: - Reciprocal intrusion/extrusion or tipping of anchorage teeth  leads to oclusal plane changes and unwanted vertical displacement - Unwanted movement if the cantilever is activated outside the intended plane

Expert basis (tutor only, never show to students): Expert 2: work backwards from the end point (hardest skill to teach); distal pocket or bony defect and referral to perio; open contact; shared decision-making based on the patient's risk appetite. Expert 1: occlusal trauma from opposing occlusion; interocclusal clearance for molar extrusion; resorption and mobility with conical roots; visualising mechanics. Expert 3: cost and duration (bonus only).
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.
Ask the student to describe the end position of the teeth before discussing mechanics.

tutorMoves.question: Looking back over the whole case, which factor had the biggest impact on how you managed the impacted second molars, and why?

authoringNotes: Source: the clinical lead's 'Tutor script Case 1.docx' (Case 1: Impacted second molars). Wording is copied verbatim except where listed here.
Reveals 5.1, 5.5 and 6.4 were shortened to fit the 60-word Help limit, pending the clinical lead's approval. Each full original is kept word for word in that phase's tutorGuidance.
Typo fixed in the full 5.1 reveal: 'alilgn' to 'align'.

Left exactly as written, to confirm with the clinical lead: the 5.2 reveal ends mid-sentence ('Some may choose to extract'); Phase 4 has no criterion 4.1; the 4.4 reveal says 'retained #84' while its criterion says '#83'.

Added for the pipeline: criterion ids sm1-<number>, accepted-extra ids, the finding title 'Clinical finding', a 'tutor only, never show to students' label on each Expert basis line and on each full reveal kept in tutorGuidance. Items over the app's 500-character limit per tutorGuidance item are split at sentence or line breaks into numbered parts, words unchanged.
